title: Does AI Tutoring Work? Size Matters
author: Alfred Essa
summary: Essa uses a Harvard study claiming AI tutors double learning gains as a prompt to argue that educators must read research through effect sizes, not p-values. He defines an effect as the change in an outcome caused by an intervention and an effect size as the magnitude of that change. Using a worked example of a tutoring programme (74 vs 69, SD 15), he calculates Cohen's d of 0.33 and translates it into grade-band shifts. His move is to make the statistic concrete for a principal deciding on resources. He closes with the caveat that causal language depends on study design, since observational effect sizes may reflect motivation or family support.
points: Statistical significance only says an effect is probably real; effect size says how big it is, and that is what a school leader needs for decisions.
A worked Cohen's d calculation (0.33 for a tutoring programme) shows how to turn raw score gaps into practical meaning.
Cohen's benchmarks (0.2, 0.5, 0.8) can be translated into letter-grade improvements, making research usable for non-statisticians.
Small effects can still matter, but they should be judged realistically against cost and implementation.
Effect sizes are only as causal as the study design behind them; without random assignment they may reflect confounds.
quotes: Yet surprisingly, many research studies still report only "statistical significance" instead of effect sizes and confidence intervals.
A p value might tell us the direction of an effect, but only an estimate of effect size tells how big it is. We should always start with effect sizes.

As a principal making a real decision, the effect size is far more important. Even though Program A is "statistically significantly better," an improvement of 0.2 grade levels might be too small to justify switching programs, especially if Program A is more expensive or requires more resources to implement.
By just looking at the raw numbers, we can see the tutoring group scored 5 points higher on average. But is 5 points a lot or a little?
Our tutoring program didn't dramatically transform student performance – it didn't turn D students into A students – but it did provide a consistent, modest boost across the grade spectrum.

Without proper experimental controls or random assignment to treatment conditions, what we measure might be correlational rather than causal. A strong effect size in an observational study might reflect not just the impact of the intervention, but also other factors like student motivation or family support.
